newsitem.title: HONG KONG: British HK general sees PLA role in unrest unlikely.
newsitem.headline: British HK general sees PLA role in unrest unlikely.

text.p: Britain's garrison commander in Hong Kong said on Sunday he was convinced China's army was unlikely to get involved in suppressing unrest after Beijing takes the colony back on July 1.

Major-General Bryan Dutton, in an interview on Hong Kong Television's Newsline programme, also predicted a smooth British military withdrawal, now in its final stages, with just five weeks to go before the handover.
When Britain transfers sovereignty to China at midnight on June 30, ending 156 years of colonial rule, the People's Liberation Army (PLA) will take over defence responsibilities in Hong Kong.

With 106 PLA troops already in position to prepare garrison facilities, and a further 90 due to arrive on Friday, the Chinese army was creating a "shop window" aimed at repairing the bad image it earned when it crushed student-led democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989, Dutton said.
"Everything I've seen so far shows they want to create a good impression," he said.

"These are very good demonstration troops," Dutton said, adding that the soldiers had clearly been carefully selected and trained to ensure their good behaviour, and that they were well equipped and wore new style modern uniforms that broke with past PLA tradition.

The PLA advance units in Hong Kong before the handover are allowed neither to bear arms nor wear their uniforms in public outside the barracks under a Sino-British aggreement on their presence in the territory.

Dutton said he believed the PLA would continue to keep a low profile in Hong Kong after the sovereignty change, having been briefed by the British that this was the garrison tradition in the territory.
He dismissed the possibility that the Chinese troops might be called in to help police suppress unrest.

"It's a very stable society and a very unlikely scenario," he said, noting that Hong Kong had become self-sufficient in maintaining law and order, and that local police were well organised to cope with trouble.

He said Hong Kong faced no serious military threat, and the PLA's main role was to demonstrate China's sovereignty, raising the flag and providing guards of honour in much the same way the British garrison had done for Britain.
China has indicated it will create a Hong Kong garrison up to 10,000-strong, although part of it may be stationed over the border in China.

Britain has already shut down most of its military sites in Hong Kong. About 1,000 military and civilian personnel, including the 400 soldiers of the Black Watch regiment, remain attached to the British garrison, down from about 10,000 a few years ago.
